intro: I started Della as an AI employee for nail salons, beginning with calls and bookings. The more I worked on it, though, the more I realized that the phone was only one part of a much larger problem: the owner is usually the person connecting all of the systems that actually run the business.
why: I started working on Della in April of 2026 as OpenOperator. I was spending a lot of time studying the foundations of AI, and around the OpenClaw moment I began learning about agentic AI and thinking that eventually, if not already, these models and agents would get better than any human across tasks on a computer. What they wouldn't know out of the box, though, was how a particular business worked and how to use the actual systems inside it.

I started looking at medspas, but the compliance side pushed me more toward nail salons because it was a similar, adjacent business. I thought communications were a place to start because leads often get lost there and there was something specific I could test: when someone asks for an appointment and Della checks the calendar, the appointment actually ends up in the salon's booking system.

The more I worked on it, the more I started thinking beyond the phone. Instead of only asking how good I could make an AI receptionist, I started asking what would happen if Della could understand what was happening across the salon and actually do work because of it.
industryIntro: Nail salons look like relatively simple businesses from the outside, but there is a surprising amount happening behind every appointment. Someone has to answer customers, manage the schedule, deal with cancellations, remember preferences, take payments, follow up with people, and keep track of what is happening across the business.
industryContext: The Census figures above cover employer nail-salon establishments. Zenoti's call data covers salons and spas rather than nail salons alone.
fragmentation: That started making more sense to me as I spent time around salons. A lot of these businesses are running through separate systems that do not really know about each other. The booking software knows the schedule, the payment system knows what someone spent, the phone has the customer conversation, and other information lives somewhere else. The owner or manager is usually the person filling in the gaps between all of it.
currentWedge: Della starts with customer communication because that is one of the most obvious places where this breaks. It can answer the phone, understand what someone needs, look at the salon's actual schedule, and help make or change an appointment while the customer is still on the phone.
bookingProblem: Early on, Della would sometimes say it had booked an appointment when it hadn't, which meant the caller could think they were booked in while the salon had nothing on its calendar, so I had to make the booking result part of the process instead of relying on what the model said had happened.
sources: A salon's cancellation policy can come from the information it has given Della, but when someone asks whether 4:30 is open, it has to check the current calendar because that answer can change between calls.
technical: The harness is basically the software around the model that lets Della use the salon's information and booking tools, remember a customer between conversations, and check whether a booking or another action actually worked instead of just trusting whatever the model says happened.
memory: During one of my test calls I told Della that I had chipped my nail, and when I called again a couple of days later it asked how my nail was doing and whether I had gone to the doctor for it.
That was cool because it wasn't starting over from zero and was able to remember something from my last conversation and bring it back up on the next call.
control: I don't want the owner to have to approve every normal booking, but I also don't want Della making decisions they never agreed to, so the owner chooses what it can handle on its own and what has to come back to them.
messages: Calls were where I started, but I don't want Della to just be a receptionist, so I'm expanding into messages and follow-up with the same customer context behind them, rather than having every conversation start over depending on how someone reaches the salon.
latency: All of those checks and lookups take time, which matters a lot when someone is waiting on the phone, so I'm working on the database and memory side to keep the calls moving without skipping the information Della needs, although some of the delay still comes from the model itself.
current: I've had calls go through the system and create appointments in Square, and I've now onboarded the first salon. Right now I'm working on making the product reliable in the situations where something does not go through or a person needs to step in.
futureExample: For example, if someone cancels tomorrow at 2:30, Della could know who has been trying to get an appointment, who usually books that service, which technician is available, and reach out before the owner ever has to think about it. If a regular customer suddenly stops coming in, the same system could notice that. Over time, I want more of those decisions and workflows to happen automatically.
thesis: As the models themselves become more capable and easier for anyone to use, I think the valuable part is increasingly going to be the context they have access to and their ability to actually operate inside a business.
direction: The long-term goal with Della is to get to a point where much of the nail salon can increasingly and ultimately run itself.
